cards.title: One-size-fits-none: segment by job, not by customer category
cards.summary: Serving distinct job-based segments with a single averaged solution fails everyone; separate them and rebuild each journey.
cards.use_when: You have multiple customer types (e.g., first-time buyers vs. repeat bulk buyers) receiving the same onboarding, offers or support flow and growth has stalled.
steps: Identify the distinct jobs held by different groups using your product. Example: SNHU's traditional-age students hired the university for a coming-of-age experience where financial aid mattered to parents; adult online learners hired it to gain credentials that improve professional prospects fast, making cost and speed central.
Map the full journey for each job from first inquiry to first purchase (and beyond) on one board, then mark every point where your process adds friction, delay or irrelevance for that job.

Remove or replace each friction point with an experience that fits the job. SNHU replaced a generic 24-hour email with a phone call in under 10 minutes, resolved aid and credit-transfer decisions in days instead of weeks, and gave each online student a personal adviser who checks in when assignments or tests go badly.

Accept that this can mean 'pretty much everything' changes, including org structure, budget priority and physical separation of the team serving the new job — SNHU moved its online team to separate offices so traditional university policies wouldn't constrain it.

Track whether the job is actually delivered, not just enrollment: SNHU treats a student as fired if it fails to deliver the credential outcome, and dials back recruiting when internal support systems can't keep up.
caveats: SNHU's growth (75,000+ online students, 10% surpluses, no tuition increases in four years) is a case example, not a benchmark you can copy.
Serving one job well may require deliberate de-prioritization of another segment — a strategic trade-off, not a free win.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 1: mine your own life for jobs
cards.summary: Unresolved jobs in your own daily life are legitimate innovation territory; your life is articulate data.
cards.use_when: You need an innovation hypothesis and have no budget for formal research, or you're a founder/operator building for a market you personally belong to.
steps: Look for a recurring struggle in your own routine — a task you dread, a workaround you've built, or a desire for progress you can't satisfy with existing products.

Treat your own frustration as a hypothesis, not proof. Khan's math videos for his cousin and Marcelo's child-care search both started as personal jobs; the videos were technically inferior to existing tutorials but were fun and conceptually clear, which is what the cousin was hiring them to do.

Note the functional, emotional and social dimensions of your job, since those often differ from what competitors optimize. Khan's cousin wanted to feel successful and low-stakes learning; Khan wanted family connection and to share his love of learning.

Validate against actual users before scaling. Sony's Morita ignored market research that said consumers wouldn't buy a non-recording tape player with earphones, and the Walkman sold 330 million-plus units — but this is an illustration of one leader's conviction, not a rule to skip research.
caveats: The Walkman example is retrospective and often cited selectively; ignoring research is survivorship-biased and not a recommended default.
A job that matters to you may still be too niche to build a business on without testing demand.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 2: hunt nonconsumption, not competitor share
cards.summary: People who use no solution at all — not competitors' customers — often hold the largest growth opportunity.
cards.use_when: Your category looks mature, saturated or price-competitive, and you suspect existing market-size data can't see untapped demand.
steps: Look for people who would benefit but buy nothing, or rely on homemade substitutes, rather than only studying customers of competing brands.

Quantify the gap if you can. Kimberly-Clark found roughly 40% of adults over 50 suffer incontinence and about one in three women over 18 experience some issue, yet only a small percentage use any incontinence product; many suffer up to two years before buying.

Diagnose why they abstain. Depend's problem was stigma: pack size and shape resembled children's diapers, and it looked bulky, white and crinkly — so people used feminine pads, avoided travel and restaurants, or disengaged socially instead.

Redesign the whole product and purchase experience around the job 'help me reclaim my life,' which meant inventing new materials so briefs looked and felt like underwear and packaging that looked like ordinary underwear with a transparent window.
Check whether you're cannibalizing yourself. The relaunch generated about $60 million in year one and 30% growth in year two without harming the existing line.
caveats: Nonconsumption is invisible in current sales data; you must deliberately look for it.
The Depend figures are the company's own research and a single launch's results, not a general benchmark.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 3: read workarounds as demand signals
cards.summary: Compensating behaviors show customers who want a job solved badly enough to build their own solution.
cards.use_when: You're scanning for unmet needs and notice customers jury-rigging spreadsheets, manual processes or odd substitutes.
steps: Immerse yourself in the customer's context; workarounds are hard to see from a distance. Look for cobbled-together substitutes, manual steps and time-consuming rituals.

Examples to pattern-match: small businesses using personal finance software as de facto bookkeeping; a parent running a household 'bank' to teach compound interest; calling restaurants and friends repeatedly to coordinate a dinner.
Translate the workaround into the underlying job — often the job is what people don't want to do (learn formal accounting, deal with bank minimums, coordinate scheduling) rather than what they want.

Design a solution that absorbs the complexity in the background, as QuickBooks did: it offered half the functionality of sophisticated accounting software at twice the price, and became the market leader by hiding journal entries and accounting language.
Remember the real competitor set expands to include the workaround itself: doing it yourself, hiring a person, spreadsheets, or a literal shoebox of receipts.
caveats: Workarounds don't guarantee willingness to buy — validate that customers will pay for removed effort or anxiety.
QuickBooks' pricing/feature trade-off is a specific case, not a formula for pricing.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 4: negative jobs — what customers don't want to do
cards.summary: Jobs framed as 'I don't want to X' are often the richest opportunities, especially where the alternative is time-consuming and anxiety-laden.
cards.use_when: You're evaluating service design, flow simplification or any category where customers tolerate a painful routine.
steps: List disliked routines in your category. Example: 'I don't want to see the doctor' for a likely strep throat — the parent wants quick relief without an unscheduled appointment, a long wait and a pharmacy delay.

Ask whether the job can be satisfied by removing the dreaded step rather than improving it. QuickMedx, the forerunner of CVS MinuteClinics, offered instant walk-in care with nurse practitioners prescribing for routine ailments like conjunctivitis, ear infections and strep throat.
Note the scale this validated: more than a thousand MinuteClinic locations inside CVS pharmacy stores across 33 states.

In ecommerce terms: negative jobs surface as 'I don't want to create an account,' 'I don't want to call support,' 'I don't want to compare 40 SKUs.' Each is a candidate for removing a step rather than adding a feature.
Pair each negative job with willingness-to-pay testing — relief from dread is often worth paying for, but you must confirm it.
caveats: Negative jobs in regulated categories (health, finance) may require new operational or legal structures, not just UX changes.
The MinuteClinic growth figures are a case illustration, not a forecast.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Job-hunting method 5: unusual uses reveal hidden jobs
cards.summary: Customers using your product off-label are showing you jobs your category doesn't acknowledge — and new revenue lines.
cards.use_when: You have a long-established product, flat growth, and suspect you're defined by a category rather than by what customers are doing with it.
steps: Observe actual use, not intended use. Church & Dwight noticed consumers adding Arm & Hammer baking soda to laundry detergent, mixing it into toothpaste, sprinkling it on carpets and leaving an open box in the fridge.

Convert each observation into a job statement. The brand now maps products to jobs like 'help my mouth feel fresh,' 'deodorize my refrigerator,' 'clean and freshen my carpets,' 'deodorize that stinky cat litter' and 'remove shower stain and mildew.'

Build or reposition products against those jobs. Arm & Hammer's original orange-box baking soda is now under 7% of its consumer revenue, meaning most of the business came from jobs discovered off-label.
Apply elsewhere: NyQuil users were taking it to sleep when not sick, so ZzzQuil stripped out the cold ingredients and sold the good night's sleep alone.
Check reviews, support tickets and search queries for off-label language; that's where unusual uses show up in ecommerce.
caveats: Non-medical off-label use can carry regulatory and safety risk; ZzzQuil required reformulating, not just marketing.
Single-brand revenue split figures are illustrative, not a target.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Sell the outcome, not the course catalog: B2B job alignment
cards.summary: When the buyer's job is to matter internally, sell subscriptions and owned outcomes around their business goals rather than discrete products.
cards.use_when: You sell to a functional buyer (HR, L&D, IT, marketing ops) whose internal credibility depends on connecting your product to executive priorities.
steps: Probe past the transaction to the buyer's real job. FranklinCovey's CEO visited nearly 400 customers before seeing the pattern: HR and learning leaders were hiring training products partly to be seen as vital contributors to company priorities like customer loyalty and growth — and products couldn't deliver that on their own.

Restructure the offer around arising jobs, not SKUs. FranklinCovey moved from selling individual courses to subscriptions giving near-unlimited access to all content, deliverable as full courses, bite-size modules or single-point lessons for a staff meeting.

Own outcomes, not just delivery. For one IT equipment client, FranklinCovey stationed a full-time coach at headquarters to enforce process improvements on every sales opportunity above $500 million — 'our deliverable is really a process, not a product,' with measurable ROI.

Use job definition to find uncontested positioning: FranklinCovey says it aims at jobs that don't have competitors — strategy-setting still goes to consulting firms, but strategy implementation and behavior change is a lane with few rivals.
Expect adjacent players to become lead sources rather than pure competitors; consulting firms now refer implementation work.
caveats: FranklinCovey's revenue path ($589M peak in 2000, $130M in 2009, $220M in 2015) is a turnaround case example, not a template.
Owning outcomes requires delivery capacity; a subscription model fails if the customer's arising job isn't actually served.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Excavate the job with timeline interviews, not feature wish lists
cards.summary: Asking recent buyers to draw their decision timeline surfaces the emotional obstacle that features and surveys miss.
cards.use_when: You have traffic but poor conversion, or focus groups keep returning feature requests that don't move sales.
steps: Interview people who already bought, and ask them to draw a timeline of how they got there rather than to rate features.

Look for what does NOT predict purchase. Moesta found no clear demographic or psychographic profile among downsizers, and none of the luxury features (squeakless floors, granite counters, 30 pages of customization options) tipped the decision — the customization checklist was actually an obstacle.

Search for the emotional blocker hiding in the details. The clue was repeated anxiety about the dining room table — a symbol of family life that made the move feel like discarding memories; one buyer needed days and multiple boxes of tissues to clear one closet.

Redesign around removing that blocker alongside the functional job. The builder shrank second bedrooms 20% to fit a classic dining table, provided moving services and two years of storage, and added an on-site sorting room for unhurried decisions.
Simplify choice architecture: replacing 30 pages of options with three finished-unit variations cut cold-feet cancellations from five or six a month to one.
Re-price to cover the added services — they raised the price $3,500 profitably, and grew 25% in 2007 while the market fell 49%.
caveats: Growth and cancellation figures come from one Detroit-area builder in a distressed market; treat as a case example.
Timeline interviews require interpretation; a single dramatic quote is not proof of the pattern.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use Jobs Theory as an integration tool for fragmented research
cards.summary: Jobs Theory tells you which pieces of existing research matter and how they fit together, without discarding your data.
cards.use_when: You already have personas, focus groups, panels and competitive analysis but they don't produce clear innovation direction.
steps: Keep your existing inputs — personas, ethnographic research, focus groups, customer panels, competitive analysis — but change the lens you view them through.

For each job, build a full narrative of the customer's circumstances, functional, social and emotional dimensions, obstacles removed and experiences sought. The book's framing: a comprehensive narrative versus a few scattered random frames of a movie.
Use the job to determine which information is needed and how it relates, so the causal mechanism of choice becomes visible.

Apply it as a leadership heuristic. LeBlanc said Jobs to Be Done 'gave us the language' for the leadership team and campus to discuss what had to change — the value was shared vocabulary and prioritization, not a research artifact.

Recheck the market-sizing implication: because jobs cut across product and customer categories, the addressable market (including nonconsumers and workaround users) can be far larger than category sales suggest.
caveats: Jobs-based segments often don't align with your existing reporting segments, which creates internal friction.
The approach doesn't supply validated market size on its own; existing data may still miss nonconsumption.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Five recurring questions to audit every offer
cards.summary: A reusable audit checklist drawn from the jobs framework to test whether your offer is built around a real job.
cards.use_when: Running a positioning, offer or roadmap review and needing a structured set of challenge questions.
steps: Ask what jobs customers are hiring your product or service to get done — in their words and circumstances, not your category label.
Ask whether distinct job-based segments exist that you are inadequately serving with a one-size-fits-none solution, and whether a segment is absorbing a compromise designed for someone else.
Ask whether your product — or a competitor's — is overshooting what customers are willing to pay for, i.e., adding features on dimensions that don't cause customers to buy.
Ask what experiences customers seek in order to make progress and what obstacles must be removed for them to succeed, mapping the whole find-purchase-use journey.

Ask what your understanding of the job reveals about your real competition — often not the brands in your category leaderboard but doing nothing, workarounds, spreadsheets, hiring a person or a household ritual.
Recruit nonconsumers, not just existing customers, into the evidence base; they see a different part of the job.
caveats: These questions surface hypotheses; each still needs testing with real customers and purchase behavior.
The nonconsumption framing is the authors' theory, and job-based segmentation may conflict with how your business is currently organized and measured.
